articles.x: Brazil ended the 2025/26 commercial year with a new record, consolidating its position as the world’s largest cotton exporter, according to ComexStat data compiled by the Brazilian Association of Cotton Growers (Abrapa). Between August 2025 and July 2026, the country shipped 3,373,941 tons of the fibre, 19% more than in the previous cycle, and reached record export revenue of US$5.3 billion. The result represents a milestone in Brazil’s expansion in the international market and reinforces the country’s role as a strategic supplier to the global textile industry. The increase represents approximately 538,500 additional tons of Brazilian cotton sold abroad and export revenues were 9% above the 2024/25 result. The result is the consequence of a transformation built over several years, driven by increased production and advances in different attributes of Brazilian cotton. “Brazil has expanded its production and gained scale, while also making progress in quality, traceability and sustainability,” said Danyella Bonfim, market intelligence and analysis coordinator at Abrapa. “This combination has strengthened the competitiveness of Brazilian cotton and, above all, the confidence of international buyers in the country’s ability to supply the market on a regular and consistent basis.” © Albrapa The performance kept Brazil at the top of the global cotton export rankings. According to data from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) presented in Abrapa’s August report, the United States ranked second in 2025/26, with 2.656 million tons, followed by Australia, with 1.241 million tons. articles.o: BPDB plans 442 MW solar plant on unused Rampal site
articles.s: The Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) plans to build a 442 MW solar power plant on unused land adjacent to the 1,320 MW Rampal thermal station in Bagerhat, at an estimated cost of BDT 24.98 billion. BPDB recently submitted its Development Project Proposal (DPP) to the Planning Commission. Th
articles.x: The Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) plans to build a 442 MW solar power plant on unused land adjacent to the 1,320 MW Rampal thermal station in Bagerhat, at an estimated cost of BDT 24.98 billion. BPDB recently submitted its Development Project Proposal (DPP) to the Planning Commission. The 685-acre site was originally earmarked for the second phase of the Rampal coal plant but lay idle after the previous Awami League government adopted a policy against building new coal-fired power stations. BPDB now plans to install the 442 MW DC solar plant on the site. The coal-based power plant located in Rampal Upazila of Bagerhat | Photo: BPDB Work is scheduled to run from September of the current 2026–27 fiscal year to June 2029. BPDB will provide BDT 3.74 billion from its own resources, while the remaining BDT 21.24 billion will come from the Power Sector Development Fund. The estimate is based on an exchange rate of BDT 123 to the US dollar. The 1,320 MW coal plant at Rampal is operational and run by Bangladesh-India Friendship Power Company Limited (BIFPCL), a joint venture equally owned by India’s state-owned NTPC and Bangladesh’s BPDB. Policy approval for the adjacent solar project was granted at a ministerial meeting after the Planning Commission sought clearance from Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury. Two senior Industry and Energy Division officials told Bonik Barta on condition of anonymity that the division sought the minister’s clearance because of past controversies surrounding the Rampal plant. Verbal approval was granted, but a Project Evaluation Committee (PEC) meeting has yet to be held, they said. articles.t: Uster 재활용 섬유 매트릭스로 순환성을 촉진합니다.
articles.o: Driving circularity with Uster recycled fiber matrix
articles.s: The two-way street for assessing mechanically recycled materials The textile industry’s commitment to circularity continues to accelerate, and mechanical recycling is viewed as a targeted approach to...
articles.x: The two-way street for assessing mechanically recycled materials The textile industry’s commitment to circularity continues to accelerate, and mechanical recycling is viewed as a targeted approach to cutting textile waste and its environmental impact. At the forefront of this drive, Uster has developed the Recycled Fiber Matrix, a two-dimensional assessment of mechanically recycled fibers to guide optimum processing and end-uses. Figure 1: Uster Recycled Fiber Matrix for mechanically recycled cotton based on L(n) and SFC(n) Recycled cotton fibers are difficult to categorize because of their inconsistency and variability. How can the industry evaluate mechanically recycled material accurately – and match it to the most suitable spinning methods and product end-uses? Help is at hand from Uster, in the form of the Recycled Fiber Matrix. It provides an objective assessment of recycled cotton, so that recyclers, spinners and brands are guided towards what can be made from it, and how. The concept fits perfectly with the industry’s need for greater circularity and transparency in recycling. The facts that matter Precise data about the physical characteristics of recycled fibers is essential to understand how they will behave in spinning and their end-use. The Uster Recycled Fiber Matrix focuses on the essential numbers – such as length of fibers (L(n)), of the longest 5% fibers (5% L(n)), and short fiber content (SFC(n)). The background to the development of the Recycled Fiber Matrix involved testing of a significant number of 100% mechanically recycled cotton fiber samples from key recycling regions, including China, India and Europe. articles.o: VeriVide expands its LED colour assessment range
articles.s: VeriVide – a member of the British Textile Machinery Association (BTMA) – is expanding its UltraView range of visual colour assessment equipment with the launch of a new compact model designed to make tuneable LED technology accessible to more organisations across textile and apparel supply chains.
articles.x: VeriVide – a member of the British Textile Machinery Association (BTMA) – is expanding its UltraView range of visual colour assessment equipment with the launch of a new compact model designed to make tuneable LED technology accessible to more organisations across textile and apparel supply chains. The new UltraView60 provides the same colour assessment technology and functionality as VeriVide’s existing UltraView system, but in a smaller and more cost-effective format for businesses that do not require a large viewing area or where laboratory space is limited. At the same time, the existing UltraView has been renamed UltraView90, creating a two-model range based around different viewing areas while retaining identical core technology and capabilities. The development comes as brands, textile manufacturers, suppliers and testing laboratories increasingly transition from conventional fluorescent lighting to LED technology for the visual assessment of colour. Fundamental consistency Consistent lighting conditions are fundamental to colour evaluation throughout textile supply chains, particularly where materials and finished products may be assessed at several different locations before reaching the consumer. Changes in lighting technology therefore need to be introduced consistently if manufacturers and their customers are to avoid discrepancies in colour approval. VeriVide, based in Leicester, UK, has specialised in controlled lighting and colour assessment for more than 60 years and developed the UltraView range to provide greater flexibility as specifications continue to evolve. articles.o: Recycled fiber demand grows faster than textile-to-textile supply
articles.s: Key global recycled fiber market projections Global production: Reached 132 million tons in 2024, with recycled fiber holding a 7.6% market share. Textile-to-Textile bottleneck: Less than 1% of globa...
articles.x: Key global recycled fiber market projections Global production: Reached 132 million tons in 2024, with recycled fiber holding a 7.6% market share. Textile-to-Textile bottleneck: Less than 1% of global fiber comes from recycled textiles, as 98% of recycled polyester relies on plastic bottles. China market growth: Projected to grow from $3.32 billion to $5.87 billion by 2030. United States market growth: Projected to grow from $2.41 billion to $4.13 billion by 2030. India waste recovery: Recovers over 95% of its 7.07 million tons of annual pre-consumer textile waste, targeting a $3.5 billion market by 2030. Figure: According to Grand View Research, the US recycled polyester market stood at $2.41 billion and is projected to reach $4.13 billion by 2030. The global recycled fiber market is moving into a strategic phase. Brands are increasing recycled-content sourcing, governments are tightening circularity rules, and textile manufacturers are investing in recycling capacity. However, the demand for recycled fiber is soaring, while the supply of high-quality textile waste remains severely limited. According to the Materials Market Report by Textile Exchange, global fiber production reached a record high of 132 million tons in 2024. Recycled fibers accounted for only 7.6% of overall output. Recycled polyester remained the dominant recycled material, making up roughly 6.9% of the total fiber market. About 98% of recycled polyester was still sourced from plastic bottles. Recent 2026 data from Textile Exchange emphasizes that breaking this bottleneck requires shifting away from open-loop bottle recycling toward localized, renewable-powered textile-to-textile processing. articles.t: 커버낫, 데님으로 짙어진 가을…‘Crafted for Autumn’
articles.o: 커버낫, 데님으로 짙어진 가을…‘Crafted for Autumn’
articles.s: 캐주얼 브랜드 커버낫(COVERNAT)이 26 FALL 캠페인 화보를 공개하고 데님을 중심으로 한 새로운 시즌 컬렉션을 선보였다.이번 컬렉션은 ‘Crafted for Autumn’을 테마로 차분한 텍스처와 견고한 디테일을 활용해 가을 특유의 깊이 있는 분위기를 표현했다. 시간과 손길의 흔적이 쌓인 목공방을 배경으로 데님과 셔츠, 럭비 티셔츠, 후드, 스웻 등을 조합해 자연스러운 가을 캐주얼 스타일을 담았다.시즌의 중심은 데님이다. 다양한 실루엣과 컬러의 데님 셔츠와 재킷, 팬츠를 구성해 간절기부터 가을까지 활용할 수 있도록 했다.

articles.o: A lighter footprint for down
articles.s: Allied Feather + Down, headquartered in Montebello, California, has announced the results of a recent carbon footprint audit conducted by Green Threads DPP at its facility in Hangzhou, China. The results show that Allied’s cradle-to-gate down processing generates 85% less carbon emissions than the e
articles.x: Allied Feather + Down, headquartered in Montebello, California, has announced the results of a recent carbon footprint audit conducted by Green Threads DPP at its facility in Hangzhou, China. The results show that Allied’s cradle-to-gate down processing generates 85% less carbon emissions than the estimated industry average. The audit focused specifically on down processing, using actual facility and supply chain data to quantify its carbon footprint. The result gives brands a more specific benchmark for evaluating the carbon impact of the down they source and the processes used to prepare it for finished products. “We’ve known for years that down plays an important role in building a more circular and lower-impact apparel value chain,” said Daniel Uretsky, president of Allied Feather + Down. “These audited results allow us to put real numbers behind that belief. The data shows that our processing methods deliver a dramatically lower carbon footprint than other down providers, giving brands objective information they can use when making material decisions.” The audit found that Allied’s processing methods generated 0.48 kg CO₂e per kg of down – about 85% lower than estimated industry averages (3.2 kg CO2e per kg) for conventional down and 57.9% lower than published figures (1.14 kg CO2e per kg) for recycled down. It also found that the carbon footprint of Allied’s down is 95% lower than the estimated carbon footprint of polyester fibres used in alternative insulations. Allied’s Hangzhou facility utilises on-site water reclamation, allowing 95% of all water to be reused, with only around 5% lost to evaporation. articles.x: Terrot Textilmaschinen will showcase its latest circular knitting technology at the 24th Egypt Stitch & Tex Expo, taking place from 24-27 September 2026 at the Cairo International Conference Center (CICC) in Nasr City, Cairo. The German textile machinery specialist, a member of Santoni China Group, will participate together with its Egyptian representative Setraco Safouh Tex, presenting the Terrot I3P 196 open-width circular knitting machine. Designed to support flexible, high-quality production, the I3P 196 addresses applications ranging from sportswear, leisurewear and fashion to technical textiles, automotive fabrics and home textiles. Terrot says the exhibition will provide an important platform to engage with manufacturers, investors and industry partners from Egypt and neighbouring textile markets, as producers respond to shorter product development cycles, sustainability requirements and growing demand for differentiated fabrics. The I3P 196 being demonstrated in Cairo is configured with a 34-inch diameter, E24 gauge and 108 feeders. articles.s: The National Institute of Textile Engineering and Research (NITER) hosted a day-long career-focused event titled ‘Thrive 2026’ on September 5, 2026, organized by the NITER Career Club (NCrC), with the aim of bridging the gap between academic life and professional careers and preparing students for t
articles.x: The National Institute of Textile Engineering and Research (NITER) hosted a day-long career-focused event titled ‘Thrive 2026’ on September 5, 2026, organized by the NITER Career Club (NCrC), with the aim of bridging the gap between academic life and professional careers and preparing students for the evolving job market. The event featured NITER National Job Fest, along with the final rounds of the Case Catalyst and Public Speaking competitions. Students from schools, colleges, and universities across the country participated in the competitions. Shawkat Aziz Russell, President of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA), attended the event as the Chief Guest, while Shorikul Islam Sarker, Vice President of BTMA, was present as the Special Guest. The Director of NITER, along with HR professionals and representatives from several reputed organizations, also attended. The first segment of the day featured the final rounds of the Case Catalyst and Public Speaking competitions. Participants demonstrated their abilities through real-world problem analysis, logical argumentation, creative thinking, and effective communication. A major attraction of ‘Thrive 2026’ was the NITER National Job Fest, where students and graduates could submit their CVs to participating organizations. The job fair also gave job seekers the opportunity to interact directly with HR representatives and discuss career opportunities, recruitment processes, and professional development. Sharing insights on CV preparation and job readiness, Md. Rajin, Executive – HR at Square, emphasized the importance of proper CV alignment and ATS-friendly resumes. articles.s: Aziz Packaging is now produceing roughly 1.5 million kraft paper cones a month for the yarn-winding stage of spinning, shipped free on board (FOB) from the Bangladesh port of Chattogram, with packaging and port handling built into the cone cost. The company, based in Narayanganj, Bangladesh, is supp
articles.x: Aziz Packaging is now produceing roughly 1.5 million kraft paper cones a month for the yarn-winding stage of spinning, shipped free on board (FOB) from the Bangladesh port of Chattogram, with packaging and port handling built into the cone cost. The company, based in Narayanganj, Bangladesh, is supplying textile spinning mills across South Asia as regional yarn production and yarn trade volumes continue to grow. The Bangladesh spinning sector produced an estimated 1.7 million tons of cotton and blended yarn in the 2024-25 financial year, with industry forecasts pointing to roughly 1.9 million tons in 2025-26, according to the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service. Nearly all of it, whether spun domestically or imported, is wound onto a paper cone before it moves further down the supply chain. The company’s cones are built as spiral-wound kraft paper constructions rather than single rolled sheets – narrow paper strips wound helically around a tapered mandrel, with adhesive between plies and the seams of adjacent layers deliberately offset. This construction, more than taper angle or surface finish alone, is what determines crush resistance and package stability as autoconer winding speeds rise industry-wide. Aziz Packaging manufactures in the two taper angles most widely used in industrial yarn winding in smooth, velvet, and embossed surface finishes, classified under HS code 4822.10.00. The company runs both manual and automatic production lines and reports compatibility with Murata, Savio and Schlafhorst autoconer platforms. “Most specification conversations stop at taper angle and finish, because those are what a buyer can see and measure,” explains Aziz MD Jafar Iqbal Bhuiyan. “The wall construction underneath is what actually decides how a cone holds up once it’s loaded

articles.o: Removing the tension from heat-setting
articles.s: Eltex, a member of TMAS, the Swedish textile machinery association, is helping textile manufacturers improve heat-setting consistency with its ACT-MULTI system, which individually monitors and automatically controls yarn tension across every yarn position. Heat-setting is a critical stage in the pro
articles.x: Eltex, a member of TMAS, the Swedish textile machinery association, is helping textile manufacturers improve heat-setting consistency with its ACT-MULTI system, which individually monitors and automatically controls yarn tension across every yarn position. Heat-setting is a critical stage in the production of synthetic and blended yarns, where precise and consistent processing conditions are required to stabilise yarn structures, lock in twist and bulk, and ensure predictable performance during subsequent processes including dyeing and finishing, weaving, knitting and tufting. The technology is particularly relevant to carpet yarn production, where carefully controlled heat treatment relieves internal stresses and improves bulk, resilience, dimensional stability and dye uptake. Variations in yarn tension during heat-setting can consequently affect both processing consistency and finished carpet quality. ACT-MULTI addresses this challenge by individually monitoring and automatically controlling yarn tension on the input side of the heat-setting machine tunnel. The system offers a fast response for precise tension control and incorporates integrated yarn break detection. An external display enables operators to monitor the complete system, while active yarn positions can be learned rapidly when new orders are introduced. Tension and stop values can be adjusted independently for each tunnel, while sensor parameters can be configured for different yarn groups. articles.t: MCPI와 IOCL이 Odisha에서 ₹5,000-Crore 폴리에스터 제조 프로젝트를 위해 손을 잡았습니다.
articles.o: MCPI and IOCL join hands for ₹5,000-Crore Polyester Manufacturing Project in Odisha
articles.s: Landmark partnership paves the way for a 900 TPD integrated polyester facility at Bhadrak, strengthening India’s domestic polyester ecosystem and advancing IOCL’s diversification into textiles MCPI Private Limited and Indian… The post MCPI and IOCL join hands for ₹5,000-Crore Polyester Manufacturing
articles.x: Landmark partnership paves the way for a 900 TPD integrated polyester facility at Bhadrak, strengthening India’s domestic polyester ecosystem and advancing IOCL’s diversification into textiles MCPI Private Limited and Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) have signed a Joint Venture (JV) Agreement to establish a ₹5,000-crore polyester yarn manufacturing facility at Bhadrak in Odisha, marking a significant milestone in the development of India’s domestic polyester value chain. The agreement was signed at IOCL’s Refinery Headquarters by Mr. Debi Prasad Patra, Managing Director & CEO, MCPI, and Mr. S.K. Papneja, Executive Director, on behalf of IOCL. The signing marks the culmination of more than a year of strategic collaboration between the two companies. The partnership follows the approval of the IOCL Board in December 2024 and final clearance from the Government of India in June 2026, paving the way for the formal creation of the joint venture and implementation of the project. The project brings together the complementary strengths of IOCL’s petrochemical capabilities and MCPI’s expertise in polyester and textiles, with the objective of creating a large-scale, technology-driven polyester manufacturing platform in Odisha. 900 TPD Continuous Polymerisation Facility At the heart of the project will be a 900 tonnes-per-day (TPD) Continuous Polymerisation (CP) unit, supported by downstream manufacturing facilities for Fully Drawn Yarn (FDY), Draw Textured Yarn (DTY) and polyester chips. These products are key building blocks for the textile industry and find applications across apparel, home textiles and industrial textiles. articles.s: At the forthcoming Aachen-Dresden-Denkendorf International Textile Conference (ADD-ITC) 2026, which will take place from November 26-27 at the International Congress Centre in Dresden, Germany, Oliver de Haas of evico GmbH will provide details of the SupraWeave project. articles.x: At the forthcoming Aachen-Dresden-Denkendorf International Textile Conference (ADD-ITC) 2026, which will take place from November 26-27 at the International Congress Centre in Dresden, Germany, Oliver de Haas of evico GmbH will provide details of the SupraWeave project. This is dedicated to fundamentally transforming circular weaving technology through the use of a superconducting weft insertion system. The goal is to process delicate, high-performance fibres such as glass and carbon on circular looms. Such fibres are indispensable in industries such as aerospace, automotive, and energy technology, but their fragility and the high mechanical stresses of conventional circular weaving processes have so far posed an insurmountable hurdle and processing is only currently possible on flatbed looms. The project’s main innovation is the use of superconducting magnetic bearings which enable frictionless, precise guidance of a levitating shuttle. This new weft insertion system is complemented by low-damage guidance of the warp and weft yarns enabling a level of material protection that has never been achieved before. A weft feeder for a Starlinger circular loom is being developed. © TU Dresden A holistic development approach is being taken in the project, ranging from the modelling of the magnetic bearings and yarn guidance to the adjustment of the fabric take-off, and on to the production and characterisation of the end products. Particular emphasis is being placed on validating the developed models and algorithms to ensure the high reliability and efficiency of the new technology. articles.o: Taking the tension out of heat-setting
articles.s: The ACT-MULTI system developed by Eltex – a member of TMAS, the Swedish textile machinery association – is bringing individual yarn tension monitoring and automatic control to the heat-setting process, helping manufacturers maintain consistent processing conditions across every yarn position. As a c
articles.x: The ACT-MULTI system developed by Eltex – a member of TMAS, the Swedish textile machinery association – is bringing individual yarn tension monitoring and automatic control to the heat-setting process, helping manufacturers maintain consistent processing conditions across every yarn position. As a critical stage in the production of synthetic and blended yarns, heat-setting relies on precise and consistent processing conditions to stabilise yarn structures, lock in twist and bulk and ensure predictable performance during subsequent processes such as dyeing and finishing, prior to, or after weaving, knitting or tufting. This is particularly important in carpet yarn production, where carefully controlled heat treatment relieves internal stresses and improves bulk, resilience, dimensional stability and dye uptake. Variations in yarn tension during the process can consequently have an impact on both processing consistency and the quality of the finished carpet. The ACT-MULTI addresses this challenge by individually monitoring and automatically controlling yarn tension on the input side of the heat-setting machine tunnel. Its fast response enables highly precise tension control and the system also incorporates integrated yarn break detection. An external display allows operators to monitor the complete system quickly and clearly, while active yarn positions can be learned rapidly when new orders are introduced. Tension and stop values can be adjusted independently for each tunnel and sensor parameters configured for different yarn groups, allowing separate settings to be applied to yarns passing through individual tunnels. articles.o: TERROT AND SETRACO SAFOUH TEX TO SHOWCASE CIRCULAR KNITTING TECHNOLOGY AT EGYPT STITCH & TEX EXPO 2026
articles.s: German textile machinery specialist presents the I3P 196 in Cairo, highlighting efficiency, versatility and sustainable textile manufacturing Terrot Textilmaschinen GmbH, a Germany-based textile machinery specialist and member of the Santoni China Group, will participate in the 24th Egypt Stitch & T
articles.x: German textile machinery specialist presents the I3P 196 in Cairo, highlighting efficiency, versatility and sustainable textile manufacturing Terrot Textilmaschinen GmbH, a Germany-based textile machinery specialist and member of the Santoni China Group, will participate in the 24th Egypt Stitch & Tex Expo, taking place from September 24 to 27, 2026, at the Cairo International Conference Center (CICC) in Nasr City, Cairo. Together with its Egyptian representative and booth host, Setraco Safouh Tex, Terrot will present the Terrot I3P 196, an open-width circular knitting machine designed to support flexible, high-quality production across sportswear, leisurewear, fashion, technical textiles, automotive applications, and home textiles. The exhibition provides Setraco and Terrot with a platform to engage with manufacturers, investors, and industry partners from Egypt and neighboring textile markets, including key regional production and sourcing hubs. The presentation of the I3P 196 reflects the companies’ focus on textile innovation, production efficiency, and responsive supply chains in a global textile market increasingly shaped by shorter development cycles, sustainability requirements, and demand for differentiated fabrics. High-performance platform for advanced fabric applications The Terrot I3P 196 on display is configured with a 34-inch diameter, E24 gauge and 108 feeders. articles.s: HSBC Bangladesh, Apparel Impact Institute (Aii), the Embassy of Sweden in Dhaka and the Delegation of the European Union in Bangladesh convened a high-level roundtable on “Advancing Decarbonization for Apparel in a Changing Energy Landscape.” The discussion brought together representatives from gove
articles.x: HSBC Bangladesh, Apparel Impact Institute (Aii), the Embassy of Sweden in Dhaka and the Delegation of the European Union in Bangladesh convened a high-level roundtable on “Advancing Decarbonization for Apparel in a Changing Energy Landscape.” The discussion brought together representatives from government, industry, global brands, financial institutions and development partners to explore how Bangladesh can accelerate the transition to reliable and competitive clean energy for its apparel sector. The event featured H.E Michael Miller, Ambassador and Head of Delegation of the European Union to Bangladesh; Olle Lundin, Chargé d’Affaires, Embassy of Sweden; Md Mahbub ur Rahman, CEO, HSBC Bangladesh; Md Sarwar Hossain, Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank; and Vidya Khan, Vice President, Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA). The discussion highlighted the importance of accelerating Bangladesh’s transition to clean energy, both to advance the decarbonization of the apparel sector and to strengthen its competitiveness, resilience and long-term growth. Two keynote presentations were delivered during the event. The first, on “Powering & Financing Bangladesh’s Apparel Transition,” was delivered by Kristina Elinder Liljas, Senior Director for Sustainable Finance and Engagement, Aii, and Kim Hellström, Senior Sustainability Manager, H&M Group. The second keynote, titled “Clean Energy Potential for Bangladesh,” was delivered by Justin Wu, Head of Sustainability and Climate Change, Asia and Middle East, and Randolph Brazier, Global Head of Clean Power Systems, Global Sustainability, HSBC. articles.o: ZDHC launches initiative to strengthen chemical and wastewater management in textile, apparel and leather industries
articles.s: A project to protect biodiversity and water resources through sustainable chemical management and wastewater management in Bangladesh’s textile, apparel, and leather industries was formally launched...
articles.x: A project to protect biodiversity and water resources through sustainable chemical management and wastewater management in Bangladesh’s textile, apparel, and leather industries was formally launched in Dhaka recently. Held at the Lakeshore Grand Hotel, the launching event brought together key representatives from government agencies, development partners, global brands, industry associations, manufacturers, and technical organizations. Figure: Dignitaries and representatives from government agencies, development partners, global brands, industry associations, and implementation partners at the launching event of the ZDHC-AFD initiative. Funded by the Agence Française de Développement (AFD) and led by the Netherlands-based Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals (ZDHC) Foundation, the 36-month initiative will support 100 textile and leather manufacturing facilities across Bangladesh in improving chemical management, wastewater performance, and sustainable production practices. The project's technical and local implementation will be jointly led by Swiss specialized firm ECOPSIS and local solution partner Amin & Jahan Corporation Ltd. During the opening remarks, Mariella Noto, Academia & Multilateral Partnerships Director at the ZDHC Foundation, emphasized that the project will look beyond factory-level compliance to address the broader systemic impacts of industrial pollution on aquatic life, biodiversity, and local communities. “Anything that we do with water will end up in the air, will end up in the soil and will affect different parts of society. It is a holistic system,” Ms. Noto stated. “What we are aiming for is long-term, sustainable, and systemic change — not something that we will do for three or four years, step out, and leave as it is. articles.s: A data-led look at a small consumable inside a large, high-speed textile production system Jafar Iqbal Bhuiyan, Managing Director, Aziz Packaging Limited, Bangladesh Article Summary: Bangladesh’s textile industry operates at enormous scale, while modern winding equipment can handle yarn at up to 2,2
articles.x: A data-led look at a small consumable inside a large, high-speed textile production system Jafar Iqbal Bhuiyan, Managing Director, Aziz Packaging Limited, Bangladesh Article Summary: Bangladesh’s textile industry operates at enormous scale, while modern winding equipment can handle yarn at up to 2,200 metres per minute. This article uses current industry and machinery data to explain why cone taper, dimensions, surface finish, roundness and batch consistency deserve to be treated as process variables—not merely packaging specifications. Figure 1. Kraft paper yarn cones used in spinning and winding applications. Image source: Aziz Packaging Limited. Bangladesh’s textile industry is a story of scale. The Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA) currently reports 1,883 member mills, including 530 yarn manufacturing mills, and estimates investment in the primary textile sector at around US$32 billion. At the downstream end of the value chain, Bangladesh recorded US$38.70 billion in apparel exports during FY 2025–26, according to Export Promotion Bureau data reported by Textile Focus. But scale also magnifies small inefficiencies. When a mill is running hundreds or thousands of spindles and high-speed winding positions, a component that costs only a few cents or taka per piece can still interact with a production system worth millions of dollars. The paper cone is one of those components. articles.s: The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, the trade body representing the country’s powerful garments sector, has suggested providing special government incentives for the first two years and setting the pension age limit, when a worker is eligible to cash in on his or her cont
articles.x: The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, the trade body representing the country’s powerful garments sector, has suggested providing special government incentives for the first two years and setting the pension age limit, when a worker is eligible to cash in on his or her contributions, for RMG workers at 55, instead of 60. BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan made the demand at a discussion on the Universal Pension Scheme was held on Saturday (September 5) at the Nurul Quader Auditorium of BGMEA Complex in Uttara, Dhaka, bringing together members and relevant stakeholders of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA). Dr. Md. Suratuzzaman, Executive Chairman of the National Pension Authority, presided over the event. The BGMEA president said that to make the scheme more attractive and popular among garment workers, he suggested providing special government incentives for the first two years. Sheikh Kamrul Hasan, Member of the National Pension Authority under the Finance Division of the Ministry of Finance, BGMEA Senior Vice President Inamul Haq Khan, and Vice President Md. Reazwan Selim spoke as special guests. In a keynote presentation, Dr. Md. Suratuzzaman said the government introduced the Universal Pension Scheme to ensure the future financial security of citizens, offering a vital safety net in old age. Citizens aged 18 to 50 can deposit contributions through banks and will receive pension returns upon reaching 60 years of age. If a subscriber dies before turning 60, their nominee will receive the deposited funds along with accrued profits. articles.o: Envoy Textiles turns shopfloor experience into an in-house scouring machine
articles.s: Envoy Textiles Limited (ETL) has developed and commissioned a fabric scouring machine through its own Engineering Division, taking inspiration from an existing machine already operating on its finishi...
articles.x: Envoy Textiles Limited (ETL) has developed and commissioned a fabric scouring machine through its own Engineering Division, taking inspiration from an existing machine already operating on its finishing floor. The initiative reduced the required investment by around 85 percent compared with purchasing a comparable commercial machine. Figure 1: Envoy Textiles team, led by Chairman Kutubuddin Ahmed, at the inauguration of the new fabric scouring machine. The machine was inaugurated on 13 August 2026 at Envoy Textiles’ factory premises by Kutubuddin Ahmed, Chairman of Envoy Textiles Limited, and Sumayyah Ahmed, Director, along with family members. Rather than starting with an entirely new machine concept, Envoy’s engineers studied the configuration and operating principles of the existing scouring machine on the production floor. They then developed a similar setup using their technical experience, locally sourced materials and available mechanical components. This approach gave the team several practical advantages: The engineering team already understood the machine’s operating principle and production requirements. The production team could operate the new machine without facing a significant learning curve. Existing materials and components could be utilized, helping reduce fabrication cost. Technical risks were comparatively lower because the design was based on a proven operating setup. According to Envoy, the new machine cost approximately 15 percent of the investment required for a comparable purchased unit. Initial trials have also shown no distinguishable difference in performance compared with the existing machine. articles.x: A special seminar titled “Advancing Bangladesh-India Textile Value Chains through Seamless Logistics and Trade Facilitation” was held today at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Exhibition Centre (BCFEC), Purbachal, Dhaka, focusing on strengthening cooperation between Bangladesh and India’s textile and apparel industries and facilitating bilateral trade. The seminar was held from 4:00pm to 5:00pm and was organised by the India-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (IBCCI), in co-association with Conference & Exhibition Management Services (CEMS-Global). The session was moderated by Jabed Ahmed, Chief Consultant of CEMS Limited. The keynote paper was presented by Mustazirul Shovon Islam, Managing Director of Sparrow Group. He said, ‘To sustain Bangladesh’s leadership in the global apparel market, we need to increase the production of value-added and higher-value products. This requires high-quality textiles, and India is one of the most accessible and important sources for these raw materials. Rather than calculating how much India or Bangladesh gains or loses, we need to find ways to work together. Our guiding principle should be – ‘One Supply Chain, Two Countries and One Global Ambition.’ He said stronger cooperation between the two countries could help build an integrated regional textile and apparel supply chain, enabling both Bangladesh and India to enhance their competitiveness in the global market. articles.s: The 25th Bangladesh Edition of the Textile Series of Exhibitions 2026 concludes today in Dhaka, marking 25 years of CEMS-Global USA and CEMS Bangladesh’s engagement with the country’s textile and appa...
articles.x: The 25th Bangladesh Edition of the Textile Series of Exhibitions 2026 concludes today in Dhaka, marking 25 years of CEMS-Global USA and CEMS Bangladesh’s engagement with the country’s textile and apparel industry. Held from September 2 at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Exhibition Centre (BCFEC), Purbachal, the four-day international event brought together global manufacturers, technology providers, suppliers, buyers and sourcing professionals, highlighting the latest developments across Bangladesh’s textile and apparel value chain. The 25th Bangladesh Edition featured three major international exhibitions: the 25th Textech Bangladesh 2026 International Expo, the 26th Dhaka International Yarn & Fabric Show 2026 - Summer Edition, and the 53rd DyeChem Bangladesh 2026 International Expo. Together, the exhibitions showcased textile and apparel machinery, automation, advanced production technologies, yarn, fabrics, trims, accessories, dyestuffs, chemicals and a wide range of technology-driven solutions for the textile and apparel manufacturing value chain. According to the organizers, the exhibition brought together around 1,475 companies from 37 countries, with more than 2,245 booths and pavilions. More than 16,000 business visitors participated in the four-day event. Meherun N. Islam, President & Group Managing Director of CEMS-Global USA & Asia-Pacific, said that Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry has undergone significant transformation over the past 25 years, making notable progress in modern technology, advanced production systems, productivity, international standards, compliance and sustainable manufacturing. At ITMA ASIA in Shanghai, KARL MAYER will once again demonstrate that it understands the challenges facing the Asian textile industry – and will present tailor-made solutions. Across Asia, rising labour, energy, and financing costs are compounded by continued price pressure from international brands. At the same time, sustainability requirements, shorter lead times, and smaller batch sizes are making the battle for margins even tougher. With its new machines and textile solutions for ITMA ASIA, KARL MAYER will directly address precisely these challenges. “Our closeness to customers in Asia helps us identify market requirements at an early stage and translate them into targeted innovations. The company will present its solutions to the challenges facing its customers at two exhibition booths in Shanghai. articles.s: 골프웨어 시장이 장기화된 소비 둔화 속에서도 브랜드별·점포별 성과가 극명하게 갈리는 양상을 보이고 있다. 주요 백화점 12개 점포의 최근 매출 실적을 살펴보면 ‘지포어’가 9개 점포에서 1위를 차지하며 독주 체제를 이어간 가운데 말본골프와 타이틀리스트가 뒤를 받쳤다. 반면 같은 브랜드라도 점포에 따라 두 자릿수 성장과 역신장이 엇갈리면서 골프웨어 시장의 경쟁축이 단순한 브랜드 인지도에서 상권별 고객 적중도와 상품 경쟁력으로 이동하고 있다.특히 눈에 띄는 것은 상위 브랜드 쏠림과 신흥 브랜드의 약진이 동시에 나타나고 있다는 점이다.

As Carnegie’s latest addition to its Biobased Xorel product line, Ape
articles.x: NEW YORK, NY — August 5, 2026 — Carnegie, a supplier of sustainable textiles and acoustical management solutions for the commercial industry, introduces Aperture Embroider, a new textile design as part of the new Crush Collection. As Carnegie’s latest addition to its Biobased Xorel product line, Aperture Embroider is made with rapidly renewable materials and 91% plant-based content, delivering durability, cleanability, and finish-free construction that Biobased Xorel is known for. Aperture Embroider, new design part of the Crush Collection | Courtesy of Carnegie Aperture Embroider brings a sense of movement and light to Biobased Xorel through finely stitched, radial bursts that feel almost like sparks across the surface. The embroidered detail adds a layer of dimension and tactility, while the open ground keeps it airy and versatile. As part of the Crush collection, Aperture Embroider is part of a lineup of fabrics created for designers who lead with color. From bold graphics and plush velvets to expressive florals, Crush was designed to mix, layer, and play, signaling Carnegie’s shift toward a brighter, bolder aesthetic while maintaining its commitment to responsible materials. Free of added finishes and harmful chemicals, Aperture Embroider is available in four colorways suited for wallcovering, upholstered walls/panels, and upholstery, pairing expressive design with the performance and sustainability standards Carnegie is known for. articles.s: MUSCATINE, IA. — August 23, 2026 — Allsteel is moving materiality from aesthetics to engineering with Levra™, its newest task chair designed for the way people work today. Developed in collaboration with ITO Design, Levra’s ergonomic engineering is cloaked in human-centric materials and anchored by
articles.x: MUSCATINE, IA. — August 23, 2026 — Allsteel is moving materiality from aesthetics to engineering with Levra , its newest task chair designed for the way people work today. Developed in collaboration with ITO Design, Levra’s ergonomic engineering is cloaked in human-centric materials and anchored by a first-of-its-kind, patent-pending frameless back architecture featuring structural knit material. Through this blend of textile innovation and ergonomic features, Levra presents a vision for the future of task seating—one where high performance and refined aesthetics merge to match the uncompromising demands of the modern workplace. What Makes Levra’s Back Special? During its development, the knit material of Levra’s back was treated as a design tool to help deliver structural integrity, adaptive flexibility, and a lighter visual expression: A suspended back softens the hard visual and physical edges of a traditional frame, while integrated lumbar support provides tactile feedback and comfort without restricting motion. The back is constructed through a precision-knit zero-waste manufacturing process. It is “fit-to-knit” directly to the chair’s specifications, entirely eliminating knit fabric cutting scrap. The knit material used in Levra’s back is made from 100% recycled materials, including up to 96% post-consumer polyester and up to 4% SEAQUAL® yarn made from upcycled marine litter. Its curated, monochromatic color palette and refined silhouette integrate seamlessly into design-forward interiors, offering a high-performance seating option that complements the visual language of modern office spaces. articles.s: NEW DELHI — September 3, 2026 — Apparel Group, a fashion and lifestyle retail conglomerate, announces the entry of Carrefour into India with the opening of the renowned retailer’s first flagship store at H&S Mall, Boulevard Walk, Greater Noida West, marking the beginning of an ambitious new chapter
articles.x: NEW DELHI — September 3, 2026 — Apparel Group, a fashion and lifestyle retail conglomerate, announces the entry of Carrefour into India with the opening of the renowned retailer’s first flagship store at H&S Mall, Boulevard Walk, Greater Noida West, marking the beginning of an ambitious new chapter for both businesses in one of the world’s most dynamic consumer markets. Mr. Nilesh Ved, Chairman of APPCORP Holding, Owner of Apparel Group and Founder of KORA Properties and Patrick Lasfargues, ED Carrefour The opening marks a defining milestone in Apparel Group’s India growth journey and its expansion into food and hypermarket retail. Bringing together Carrefour’s international retail expertise and Apparel Group’s deep understanding of the Indian market, the partnership sets the foundation for a new generation of modern retail in India, built around quality, value, convenience and the evolving aspirations of Indian consumers. Spanning more than 50,000+ sq. ft., the Greater Noida flagship introduces Carrefour’s established retail experience to India through a proposition thoughtfully adapted for the local market. The store features more than 15,000+ SKUs, including exclusive international products, alongside an extensive selection of locally sourced products across fresh produce, grocery, bakery, household essentials and personal care. More than a first store, the flagship signals the scale of the ambition ahead. Apparel Group plans to expand Carrefour’s presence across North India over the coming years, building a nationwide retail platform supported by strong local partnerships, modern supply chain capabilities and an integrated omnichannel ecosystem. articles.s: MOBILE, AL — September 2, 2026 — What began as Brown & Brown, a fabric and textile business founded on the Gulf Coast in 1877 and developed into Engineered Textile Fabrics in 1980, has spent nearly 150 years growing, adapting, and expanding into markets its founders could not have imagined. articles.x: MOBILE, AL — September 2, 2026 — What began as Brown & Brown, a fabric and textile business founded on the Gulf Coast in 1877 and developed into Engineered Textile Fabrics in 1980, has spent nearly 150 years growing, adapting, and expanding into markets its founders could not have imagined. Today, that company — now known as Environmental Textile Products (ETP) — is marking its next chapter with a new name, a unified brand identity, and a new website at EnvironmentalTextileProducts.com. The ETP family of brands — Environmental Textile Products, ETP Environmental, ETP ArtCraft Awnings, ETP Sports, ETP Racemarks, and ETP Industrial — united under one identity for the first time. The formal adoption of the Environmental Textile Products name reflects the full scope of the company’s evolution over the past several decades. From its roots in cut-and-sew manufacturing, ETP has expanded to serve customers across five distinct markets: environmental and containment systems, industrial fabric solutions, ArtCraft Awnings, Racemarks, and competitive track and field through ETP Sports, a specialized brand serving the high school, collegiate, and elite racing community. The new brand unites all five divisions under one identity for the first time, giving customers and partners a clearer picture of the company’s reach and capabilities. “This company has been in our family for five generations, and in that time, we’ve expanded into markets and capabilities that go well beyond where we started,” said Ken Robinson, owner of Environmental Textile Products. “The new name and brand reflect everything we do and everything we’ve built. articles.s: 뉴욕 컨템포러리 디자이너 브랜드 조이그라이슨(JOY GRYSON)이 지난 1일 신세계백화점 강남점 매장을 확장 리뉴얼 오픈했다.이번 리뉴얼은 기존 매장 규모를 확대하고 MD 구성을 새롭게 재편해 보다 다양한 컬렉션을 한 공간에서 만나볼 수 있도록 한 것이 특징이다. 기존 핸드백 중심의 구성에서 의류 라인 섹션을 강화해 조이그라이슨의 스타일을 보다 폭넓게 제안한다.조이그라이슨 역시 이번 신세계백화점 강남점 리뉴얼을 통해 고객 접점을 확대하고 제품뿐만 아니라 브랜드가 추구하는 스타일과 감성을 경험할 수 있도록 공간을 재구성했다. 핸드백

articles.o: 렉토, 덜어냄으로 완성한 '절제의 미학'
articles.s: 패션 브랜드 렉토(RECTO)가 9월 3일 2026 가을·겨울 컬렉션 ‘AS IT STANDS’를 선보인다.이번 컬렉션은 완벽하게 다듬어진 상태보다 각각의 소재와 형태가 본래 지닌 성질과 흔적을 그대로 남겨두는 것에서 출발했다. 인위적인 완성도를 더하기보다 불필요한 요소를 걷어내고 그 안에 감춰져 있던 본질을 드러내는 데 초점을 맞췄다.렉토는 소재 본연의 물성과 흔적, 형태가 가진 고유한 성질을 하나의 디자인 표현으로 받아들였다. 무엇인가를 계속 더하는 방식 대신 적절한 지점에서 멈추는 선택을 통해 이번 시즌이 지향하는 절제된 미학

articles.o: Unichem acquires Loomia
articles.s: South Korean materials manufacturer Unichem is acquiring US flexible electronics specialist Loomia Technologies as it looks to move into tactile sensing systems for humanoid robots and smart automotive interiors. The deal follows Loomia’s collaboration with Chinese automotive technology and manufact
articles.x: South Korean materials manufacturer Unichem is acquiring US flexible electronics specialist Loomia Technologies as it looks to move into tactile sensing systems for humanoid robots and smart automotive interiors. The deal follows Loomia’s collaboration with Chinese automotive technology and manufacturing group R&Y on a new flexible tactile sensor designed to detect both vertical pressure and shear forces – the lateral forces generated when an object moves across a surface. Such multi-directional sensing is considered important for humanoid robotic hands and grippers, where detecting pressure alone provides only limited information about how securely an object is being held. Loomia and R&Y are targeting the delivery of a first engineering sample of the new sensor in January 2027, with Tesla Optimus, OpenAI, Boston Dynamics, 1X and Meta among the global robotics and AI companies identified as potential customers for the technology. Based in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, Unichem has around 50 years of experience in natural leather and other materials and is an established supplier of automotive interior materials. It has agreed to acquire 100% of Brooklyn, New York-based Loomia in a transaction valued at up to $6.3 million. The acquisition is expected to combine Unichem’s materials processing expertise with Loomia’s flexible electronics technology and R&Y’s automotive-scale engineering and manufacturing capabilities. articles.o: Industry leaders call for stronger innovation ecosystem for sustainable textile growth
articles.s: Industry leaders, academics, and representatives from the apparel buying community gathered yesterday (September 2) at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Exhibition Center, Purbachal, Dhaka, for a time...
articles.x: Industry leaders, academics, and representatives from the apparel buying community gathered yesterday (September 2) at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Exhibition Center, Purbachal, Dhaka, for a timely discussion on building a stronger innovation ecosystem for Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry. The session, titled “Building Innovation Ecosystem for a Sustainable Textile & Apparel Industry,” was held as part of TexTIMe – Textile Today’s Episode 29 and the 7th episode of the Series of Exhibitions 2026, concurrently with the 25th Textech Bangladesh 2026 International Expo and the 53rd Dye+Chem Bangladesh International Expo 2026. Figure 1: Panelists of TexTIME Episode 29. The session brought together key stakeholders from industry, academia, technology and buying houses to discuss the evolving needs of Bangladesh’s textile and apparel sector and the importance of innovation in securing its future competitiveness. The panel featured Dr. Md. Hasib Uddin, Director, BGMEA and Managing Director, APS Knit Composite Ltd.; Mohammad Rashed, Vice Chairman, BKMEA and Managing Director of Pacific Sweater Ltd.; Prof. Dr. Engr. Ayub Nabi Khan, Vice Chancellor, BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT); and Mohammed Zakir Hossain, Senior Vice President, Bangladesh Garment Buying House Association (BGBA) and Chairman, TexSolution Consulting Bangladesh Ltd. The discussion was moderated by Dr. Mohammad Hasan, Managing Director, Cotton Group and Executive Editor, Textile Today, who also delivered the keynote address. The event highlighted the growing importance of creating stronger connections among industry, academia, technology providers and other stakeholders to drive innovation across the textile and apparel value chain. articles.o: Global garment trade hits $546.8 billion as synthetic fibers gain ground
articles.s: Global knit and woven garment exports reached $546.8 billion in 2025. The market has also changed significantly. Synthetic fibers are gaining a larger share. Bangladesh and Vietnam have also become ma...
articles.x: Global knit and woven garment exports reached $546.8 billion in 2025. The market has also changed significantly. Synthetic fibers are gaining a larger share. Bangladesh and Vietnam have also become major players alongside China. Figure: Cotton’s share of global fiber demand fell from 68.3% in 1960 to 21.1% in 2025. Synthetic fibers moved in the opposite direction. Their share increased from 4.6% to 71.7% during the same period. According to the August 2026 issue of The Textiles Observer, published by the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC), global textile exports grew from about $560 billion in 2006 to $914 billion in 2025. Knit and woven garment exports rose from $303.7 billion to $546.8 billion during the same period. This was an 80% increase. Knit garment exports reached $289.1 billion in 2025. They were $145.2 billion in 2006. Woven garment exports also grew. They increased from $158.5 billion to $257.7 billion. Together, knit and woven garments made up nearly 60% of global textile exports in 2025. Bangladesh moves up The growth has changed the global competitive landscape. China remained the world’s largest textile and garment exporter. Bangladesh made a major jump. It moved from 14 th place in 2006 to second in 2025. Vietnam also moved up. It rose from 21 st place to third. Together, China, Bangladesh and Vietnam accounted for about 44% of global textile exports in 2025. For Bangladesh, this shows its strong position in global apparel. But another major shift is taking place. Future growth is increasingly moving toward products that use man-made and synthetic fibers. articles.t: 런던 스타트업, PFAS 텍스타일 코팅의 대안으로 bio-based 개발
articles.o: London startup develops bio-based alternative to PFAS textile coatings
articles.s: London-based Demeter Bio has developed a bio-based coating that could help textile manufacturers replace per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) without turning to microplastic-based alternatives....
articles.x: London-based Demeter Bio has developed a bio-based coating that could help textile manufacturers replace per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) without turning to microplastic-based alternatives. Figure: From left to right - Caitlin Byrne, Adelya Khayrova, Emmanuel Asare, and Rayan Osseiran from the Demeter Bio team The company’s Fibrepel, formerly known as AguaShield, is designed to provide water and stain repellency for textiles and packaging. It can be used in applications including clothing, upholstery, hygiene products and packaging. Demeter Bio won the environment category of the Royal Society of Chemistry’s (RSC) 2026 Emerging Technologies Competition for the technology. The company began developing Fibrepel in 2024 as PFAS restrictions increased across Europe. Its founders said they found that some PFAS-free alternatives relied on microplastics and did not offer strong oil and alcohol resistance. Fibrepel uses biomaterials to target these performance gaps while avoiding PFAS and fluorinated chemistry. Demeter Bio says the technology can be adapted for different products and has potential for wider industrial applications. Rayan Osseiran, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Demeter Bio, said the technology is designed to support a shift toward PFAS-free materials rather than focusing only on removing PFAS from the environment.

A delegation of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) board, led by its president, Mahmud Hasan Khan, met President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir at Bangabhaban on Wednesday. The meeting discussed the overall situation of the ready-made garment (RMG) sector, a key driver of the national economy, emerging challenges, strengthening Bangladesh’s position in international markets and various policy issues related to protecting domestic industries. Thanking the current government for its various forward-looking and industry-friendly measures to promote domestic industries and businesses, the BGMEA president said decisions such as extending the LDC graduation timeline in view of global economic realities, providing a special BDT 200 billion financing facility to reopen inactive and closed garment factories, facilitating the procurement of bonded raw materials and direct exports for non-bonded factories, and simplifying customs procedures had particularly encouraged industry entrepreneurs. During the meeting, the BGMEA president briefed the president on the current difficult realities and challenges facing the RMG sector. The president listened attentively to their views and described the garment industry as one of the main “backbones” of the national economy. articles.o: Standard Wool investing in UK wool processing’s future
articles.s: A major investment in new wool scouring technology is taking shape at Standard Wool’s Thomas Chadwick & Sons operation in Dewsbury, West Yorkshire, strengthening one of the increasingly scarce industrial links between Britain’s sheep farms and its textile manufacturing sector. Installation of the ne
articles.x: A major investment in new wool scouring technology is taking shape at Standard Wool’s Thomas Chadwick & Sons operation in Dewsbury, West Yorkshire, strengthening one of the increasingly scarce industrial links between Britain’s sheep farms and its textile manufacturing sector. Installation of the new equipment has been progressing throughout the summer at Eastfield Mills, where Thomas Chadwick & Sons has been processing wool since 1864. Standard Wool’s latest update, issued on August 27th, shows the scale of the work now underway as the company moves towards commissioning. Large-scale wool scouring capacity has become increasingly concentrated internationally, with much of the world’s raw wool now shipped to China for cleaning and subsequent processing. Essential first stage Scouring is the essential first industrial processing stage after wool has been removed from the sheep. Raw or greasy wool contains wool grease, dirt, salts, dust and other contaminants which must be removed before the fibre can move on to subsequent textile processes. The operation involves continuously passing the wool through a series of washing and rinsing bowls before drying and further cleaning. Typically, contaminants can account for some 35-40% of the weight of greasy wool, making effective scouring critical to both the quality and economics of subsequent processing. © Standard Wool It is also an energy, water and capital-intensive operation requiring considerable specialist expertise – factors which have contributed to the migration of much of the world’s scouring capacity towards larger international processing centres. articles.s: GREENSBORO, N.C. — September 3, 2026 — Cone Denim, a global denim innovator, today announced strategic transformation plans designed to better serve the global denim fabric market. The plans include strengthening Cone Denim’s focus on its established manufacturing platform in Mexico and the planned
articles.x: GREENSBORO, N.C. — September 3, 2026 — Cone Denim, a global denim innovator, today announced strategic transformation plans designed to better serve the global denim fabric market. The plans include strengthening Cone Denim’s focus on its established manufacturing platform in Mexico and the planned exit of denim manufacturing operations in China by year-end 2026. This repositioning follows a comprehensive review of the global denim market, Cone’s manufacturing footprint, customer sourcing needs, and long-term business strategy. The decision follows careful consideration of economic, market, and geopolitical factors that have increasingly affected the competitiveness and long-term sustainability of operating denim manufacturing in China. Changing global trade dynamics, evolving customer sourcing strategies, cost pressures, supply chain considerations, and broader geopolitical developments all contributed to this determination. “We are positioning Cone Denim for its next chapter of success, with a clear priority to continue delivering for our customers with the quality, innovation, reliability, and service that have defined Cone Denim for generations,” said Steve Maggard, President of Cone Denim. “Closing the China facility was a difficult but necessary decision as we position Cone Denim for long-term competitiveness in a changing global market. articles.s: Karl Mayer will showcase a wide range of new warp knitting, warp preparation and technical textile technologies at ITMA Asia 2026, combining two exhibition stands in Shanghai with a major product show at its manufacturing site in Changzhou. The company says its latest developments have been designed
articles.x: Karl Mayer will showcase a wide range of new warp knitting, warp preparation and technical textile technologies at ITMA Asia 2026, combining two exhibition stands in Shanghai with a major product show at its manufacturing site in Changzhou. The company says its latest developments have been designed specifically to address the challenges facing textile manufacturers across Asia, where rising labour, energy and financing costs are being compounded by continued price pressure from international brands. Sustainability requirements, shorter lead times and smaller batch sizes are adding further pressure on margins. Karl Mayer will present warp knitting technologies in Hall 4.1, Booth C18 at the National Exhibition and Convention Center (NECC) Shanghai, while its warp preparation machinery will be shown in Hall 3, Booth A24. Further machine premieres will be demonstrated during an accompanying product show at Karl Mayer China in Changzhou. © Karl Mayer “Our closeness to customers in Asia helps us identify market requirements at an early stage and translate them into targeted innovations,” said Lutz Wolf, CEO of Karl Mayer. “That is why, at this trade fair, we will be showcasing solutions that are not only technologically leading but, above all, deliver one key benefit: they create measurable added value and long-term growth opportunities for our customers.” In warp knitting, Karl Mayer will introduce a new generation of tricot machines building on the cost-effective range that helped stimulate significant growth in the Chinese market during the late 2010s. articles.o: Looking beyond the runway at Manchester Fashion Week
articles.s: Manchester Fashion Week returns with a four-day programme held from September 9-12 2026 across the city’s St John’s neighbourhood, uniting designers, brands, manufacturers, educators and innovators around an industry under pressure to change. The programme is organised around a set of problems the s
articles.x: Manchester Fashion Week returns with a four-day programme held from September 9-12 2026 across the city’s St John’s neighbourhood, uniting designers, brands, manufacturers, educators and innovators around an industry under pressure to change. The programme is organised around a set of problems the sector has been slow to confront. Rather than a schedule of trend forecasting and brand showcases, the four days will work through synthetic fibre dependency, the economics of where clothes are made, who makes them and under what conditions, and what the industry’s rush toward AI actually costs. Changing Narratives opens the week on Wednesday September 9 th at the point of production, with ‘Near, Far and Number 10 North’ examining the balance between nearshoring, offshore manufacturing and supply chain resilience. The day will move through regenerative materials and next-generation animal-free innovation, before confronting the realities of fashion’s global workforce and how environmental progress can be made without displacing the livelihoods that depend on it. Changing Behaviour follows on Thursday 10 th with ‘The Polyester Paradigm’, exploring fashion’s dependence on synthetic fibres and the innovations attempting to break it. The day will move through repair, resale and take-back models, the independent businesses holding on to space in city centres, and the accessibility gap in adaptive design. Changing Industry on Friday turns to the systems beneath the product, from data and traceability in ‘The Data Thread’ to values-driven leadership in ‘Leading with Purpose’, and a series of sessions on how AI, 3D technology and automation are reshaping the way fashion is designed, produced and sold. ‘The Cost of Creativity’ will address the financial reality of building a career as

articles.o: Denim needs to look beyond carbon and rethink water efficiency as part of decarbonization
articles.s: Bangladesh does not grow cotton. Yet water may ultimately decide the country’s competitiveness in global denim sourcing. Before diving deeper, it is important to recognize that freshwater represent...
articles.x: Bangladesh does not grow cotton. Yet water may ultimately decide the country’s competitiveness in global denim sourcing. Before diving deeper, it is important to recognize that freshwater represents only 2.5% of the world’s water, and we are doing everything with this limited resource. Of that 2.5%, only approximately 33% is available for daily uses such as drinking, washing, and textile processing. This apparent contradiction reveals a deeper truth about sustainability in textiles: carbon emissions in denim manufacturing are not generated in isolation, they are driven by water. Water that is pumped, heated, circulated, treated, and discharged consumes enormous amounts of energy. In Bangladesh, where denim production is heavily dependent on wet processing and fossil fuel-based utilities, water has become the hidden engine of carbon emissions. Following earlier discussions on carbon cost and environmental price wars in denim, this article explores how water management now defines carbon intensity, operational cost, and long-term viability of Bangladesh’s denim industry. Following earlier discussions on carbon cost and environmental price wars in denim, this article explores how water management now defines carbon intensity, operational cost, and long-term viability of Bangladesh’s denim industry. Understanding the water–carbon Link In textile manufacturing, carbon and water are inseparable. Every cubic meter of water used in a denim mill triggers a chain of emissions. Groundwater extraction requires electricity, which creates carbon emissions, while heating water depends on gas or steam and therefore adds further carbon impacts. articles.o: EU’s Digital Product Passport creates new opportunity for African textiles
articles.s: The European Union’s Digital Product Passport (DPP) is creating a new opportunity for African textile and apparel manufacturers to improve traceability, circularity and access to the European market....
articles.x: The European Union’s Digital Product Passport (DPP) is creating a new opportunity for African textile and apparel manufacturers to improve traceability, circularity and access to the European market. Figure:EU’s Digital Product Passport creates new opportunity for African textiles The European Commission launched the DPP Registry and testing environment on July 20, 2026, marking a major step toward making the system operational for businesses. The Registry will record unique product identifiers, registration data and key metadata, while detailed product information will remain with economic operators or their DPP service providers. For textile and apparel companies, the development is important because the sector is one of the EU’s priority product groups under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR). The European Commission currently expects to adopt the textile-specific ESPR delegated act in the fourth quarter of 2027. A DPP could provide information on a garment’s product identification, fiber composition, origin, relevant economic operators, repair and maintenance, reuse, recycling and end-of-life management. A QR code or another data carrier on the product can provide access to the required information. For African manufacturers, this shift could turn sustainability compliance into a competitive opportunity. Better digital records can help exporters demonstrate product origin, material composition and environmental performance while building stronger links with European buyers. The opportunity is particularly relevant as African textile producers seek to expand their role in global value chains. articles.t: 날짜를 적으세요: 섬유 EPR이 실제로 작동하도록 만들기
articles.o: Put a date on it: making textile EPR work in practice
articles.s: BY IWTO BRUSSELS – Two major pieces of EU legislation are moving into implementation at the same time, and textiles sit at their intersection. Member States must transpose the revised Waste Framework Directive, which requires textile Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes to be established b
articles.x: BY IWTO BRUSSELS – Two major pieces of EU legislation are moving into implementation at the same time, and textiles sit at their intersection. Member States must transpose the revised Waste Framework Directive, which requires textile Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes to be established by April 2028. Meanwhile, the European Commission is developing textile-specific rules under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), including requirements for a Digital Product Passport (DPP). The two frameworks are designed to work together. Under the Waste Framework Directive, producer contributions are based on product weight and, where appropriate, quantity – the number of products placed on the market. These contributions finance collection, sorting, reuse, recycling and other end-of-life responsibilities. Fees must then be eco-modulated using relevant sustainability and circularity criteria developed under ESPR or other harmonised EU rules. This is an important step. But there is still a missing piece: evidence of what happens to garments in real life. Ecodesign rules are necessarily set before a product is sold. They therefore use tests, product characteristics and assumptions to predict durability, recyclability and likely lifetime. Yet technically durable clothing is not always worn for a long time. Fit, care, fashion cycles, price, resale and many other factors influence when a garment leaves use. Prediction is necessary, but it should not be mistaken for proof. A practical feedback loop IWTO proposes adding the year of production to the textile Digital Product Passport. Combined with statistically robust waste audits, this would allow authorities to see how quickly – or slowly – different categories of garments enter collection and waste streams.

Gopalakrishnan Showcasing AI-powered automation, digital factory solutions and next-generation process intelligence at INDIA ITME 2026 As the global textile industry navigates rising sustainability expectations, increasing production costs and growing pressure for operational excellence, digital automation has emerged as the defining force behind the next generation of textile processing. Textile manufacturers today are seeking far more than standalone automation—they require integrated, intelligent ecosystems capable of optimizing entire manufacturing operations through data, connectivity and artificial intelligence. Positioned at the forefront of this transformation is ELİAR Elektronik, one of the world’s leading specialists in textile wet processing automation. With over four decades of innovation, the Turkish company has evolved from a manufacturer of electronic controllers into a comprehensive provider of intelligent automation, automated dosing systems and digital factory software. As ELİAR continues to expand its global footprint, India has emerged as one of the company’s most strategic markets, driving both business growth and long-term innovation. This commitment will once again be on display at INDIA ITME 2026, where ELİAR will introduce its latest technologies designed to help textile processors achieve higher productivity, greater sustainability and intelligent decision-making through AI-driven automation. articles.o: Print Tech Bangladesh 2026 to spotlight textile printing and print technology solutions
articles.s: The 10th Print Tech Bangladesh will bring printing technology suppliers, manufacturers and industry buyers together in Dhaka from September 24–26, 2026. The three-day trade show will take place at the...
articles.x: The 10th Print Tech Bangladesh will bring printing technology suppliers, manufacturers and industry buyers together in Dhaka from September 24–26, 2026. The three-day trade show will take place at the International Convention City Bashundhara (ICCB). The event will showcase technologies and solutions for textile and garment printing, digital printing, screen printing and sublimation printing. It will also cover pre-press, print finishing, postpress, inks, consumables, software, labels and paper converting. The exhibition comes as Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry looks to improve product value, flexibility and production efficiency. New printing technologies can help manufacturers meet demand for customized designs, shorter production runs and faster turnaround. Visitors will include textile and garment manufacturers, exporters, factory owners, purchase managers, production professionals, R&D teams, quality controllers, brand managers, label printers and packaging professionals. Print Tech Bangladesh has previously been held in 2023, 2024 and 2025. The 2026 edition will mark its 10th edition, bringing a wider range of printing and related technologies under one platform. With printing playing a growing role in apparel value addition and product differentiation, the exhibition is expected to offer Bangladesh’s manufacturers a platform to assess technologies that can support the next stage of industry growth.

CAMX 2026 – the Composites and Advanced Materials Expo – will take place f
articles.x: Unimat, manufactured by James Cropper Advanced Materials, has been shortlisted for the CAMX 2026 Unsurpassed Innovation Award, recognising breakthrough technologies that advance the composites and advanced materials industry. CAMX 2026 – the Composites and Advanced Materials Expo – will take place from September 21-24, at the Georgia World Congress Centre in Atlanta, Georgia. Developed using Vectis, James Cropper’s proprietary fibre alignment technology, Unimat is a highly aligned discontinuous carbon fibre material engineered from recycled and production-induced waste carbon fibre feedstocks. It was developed through a strategic collaboration between James Cropper Advanced Materials and Carbon Fiber Recycling (CFR) in the UK, creating a scalable pathway for transforming carbon fibre waste into high-value composite reinforcement. The nomination highlights a significant industry achievement, demonstrating that recycled carbon fibre can deliver the performance, consistency and manufacturing readiness required for demanding composite applications, without sacrificing sustainability goals. Working alongside industry partners committed to improving sustainability within aerospace, Carbon Fiber Recycling applies its proprietary recovery and refinement technologies to transform carbon fibre waste into a high-quality feedstock. James Cropper subsequently uses Vectis technology to create up to 95% alignment in Unimat. “Through our collaboration with CFR, we have shown that recycled carbon fibre can be transformed into an industrially scalable material suitable for some of the most demanding composite applications,” said Lauren Wolstencroft, head of marketing at James Cropper. articles.o: Resil Chemicals: Creating the Chemistry for Tomorrow’s Textiles
articles.s: By K. Gopalakrishnan With a chemical portfolio spanning fibres, yarns, fabrics and garments, Resil Chemicals is strengthening its position as an innovation-led textile technology company. At India ITME, the company… The post Resil Chemicals: Creating the Chemistry for Tomorrow’s Textiles appeared fi
articles.x: By K. Gopalakrishnan With a chemical portfolio spanning fibres, yarns, fabrics and garments, Resil Chemicals is strengthening its position as an innovation-led textile technology company. At India ITME, the company will showcase advanced solutions in textile finishing, technical textiles and sustainable processing, while highlighting the evolving convergence of chemistry, machinery and digitalisation. Ganesh Srinivasan, CEO, Resil Chemicals For Resil Chemicals, the future of textile chemistry lies increasingly in customization, technology and sustainability. As competition intensifies in conventional textile chemicals, the Bengaluru-based company is focusing on differentiated products, intellectual property, certified solutions and closer partnerships with brands and manufacturers. The strategy is already reflected in its portfolio. Resil is a major Indian manufacturer of silicone-based textile chemicals and resins, while its solutions extend across fibres, yarns, sewing threads, woven and knitted fabrics, garments and technical textiles. The company has also expanded into polyurethane chemistry, opening new opportunities in technical textiles and sustainable finishing. Speaking about the company’s innovation-led approach, Ganesh Srinivasan, CEO, Resil Chemicals, says “Competing solely on commodity chemicals and conventional technologies will not deliver sustainable, long-term growth.” he notes, highlighting the company’s focus on creating customized and “blue ocean” opportunities. Innovation at the Core Resil’s technology strategy is built around four pillars: product innovation, service excellence, sustainability, and trusted brand value.
